title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N = 500 distinct synthetic intents (one shared initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 (computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5)). An exploratory paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (predeclared exploratory). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, provide representative per‑episode verifier diagnostics for the repaired pairs, and point readers to the archived evidence bundle for complete machine‑readable artifacts.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration can greatly reduce manual effort, but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Large language models (LLMs) are promising for intent translation, yet hallucination and factual errors remain central reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N = 500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI with an explicit small‑discordant‑count caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces for the repaired episodes, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and practical external‑validity limits.
sections.related_work:
Three converging literatures motivate a GVR architecture for NetOps reliability. First, surveys and systems work document active interest in LLMs for intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration while emphasizing hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers [1,2]. Intent‑driven configuration prototypes demonstrate feasibility but typically pair generators with ad‑hoc validation or operator oversight rather than large, controlled trials against deterministic verifiers [3]. These studies establish that translation quality alone is insufficient for operational acceptance and motivate tool‑augmented pipelines that embed deterministic validation as a gate.

Second, methodological and tool‑integration work advocates explicit generate‑validate‑repair evaluation practices and standardized validator semantics. Recent methodological blueprints call for measuring verifier coverage, failure modes, and orchestration costs rather than only generator fidelity; they emphasize end‑to‑end trial designs that preserve pairing between conditions, the value of frozen preregistration, and quantifying model‑call overhead per avoided unsafe change [2].

Third, deterministic network configuration verification tools and scalable verifiers provide concrete oracles for many syntactic and workflow properties. Prior work on scalable verifiers shows that automated checks can detect availability/sequence and policy violations at scale, but verifiers differ in which control‑plane or vendor semantics they model and therefore in the hazards they can detect [4]. Our study uses a deterministic verifier that implements canonical parsing, required‑sequence/workflow checks, availability/group constraints, paired‑field dependency enforcement, and final‑state comparison for the synthetic intent grammar; we acknowledge, as prior work does, that verifier pass does not imply absence of vendor‑specific or timing hazards.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan: The study was preregistered under the identifier study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and the analysis executor were frozen prior to execution. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as a descriptive interval.

Generation and orchestration: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini with a fixed generation configuration. The GVR controller validated that shared candidate with a deterministic verifier and, if verification failed, invoked at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The baseline condition accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. Provider accounting recorded hosted model call events totaling 504 model calls (500 shared initial calls and 4 repair calls).

Deterministic verifier semantics and codebook: The primary verifier implements a deterministic validation pipeline on a normalized CLI sequence: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change patterns); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison with the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the verifier emits a normalized configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list, and a boolean valid. A human‑readable verifier codebook maps violation codes to short descriptions; per‑episode verifier traces that include recorded violation codes and diagnostic fields are archived in the evidence bundle for inspection.

Repair policy and prompt semantics: If the verifier fails a shared_initial candidate, the GVR controller issues at most one repair prompt to the same generation model using a constrained repair template that includes: (a) the original intent abstraction; (b) the verifier violation codes and short descriptions; and (c) a request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. A repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid = true for the subsequent candidate. Repair invocations and their acceptance are logged per episode in the archived run.
sections.results:
Execution and primary counts: The run completed 1,000 episodes (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504. The observed success counts were baseline 496/500 (0.992) and guarded 500/500 (1.000), producing the paired contingency counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; all four repair attempts resulted in subsequent verifier passes and correspond to the four discordant pairs. Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008; for repaired pairs the observed model calls per pair = 2 (shared initial + one repair call).

Exact McNemar implementation and numeric reproducibility: The preregistered conditional exact McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin n = n10 + n01 and uses the two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 with success probability 0.5. For our observed contingency (n = 4, k = 4) the one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling yields the two‑sided p = 0.125. The exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016]. The preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar; therefore we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance despite the nonzero exploratory CI.

Repaired‑episode enumeration: The four repaired/discordant pairs correspond to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. For concise inspection we report the artifact‑grounded per‑pair summaries below (verifier violation code strings and short descriptions are recorded verbatim in the archived per‑episode traces):

- pair-000090 | violation_codes: [MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD] — "VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 | violation_codes: [MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK] — "Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 | violation_codes: [PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE] — "MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface's MTU change (paired‑field dependency)." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 | violation_codes: [GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT] — "Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups availability constraint." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.

Representative per‑episode verifier diagnostics (normalized configuration, violation codes, parsed/required command counts, and repair prompt/response transcripts for repaired episodes) are archived in the evidence bundle for audit and independent reproduction. The reported numeric totals and contingency counts are derived from those archived artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and reconciliation of inferential outcomes: The GVR pipeline prevented four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted. Under the preregistered exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but requires caution: McNemar conditions on observed margins and evaluates the binomial tail of discordant outcomes; with only four discordants the exact test yields the preregistered p = 0.125. The bootstrap resamples pairs without fixing margins and can produce a nonzero lower CI bound when most pairs are concordant and a small number of discordant pairs consistently favor one direction across resamples. Because the bootstrap was predeclared exploratory and small discordant counts reduce frequentist coverage guarantees for percentile intervals, we present both perspectives and follow the preregistered decision rule for the primary claim.

Verifier coverage, blind spots, and operational sufficiency: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. These checks are necessary for detecting a broad class of syntactic and workflow errors that LLMs commonly produce for our intent grammar, and they were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes in this run. However, the verifier intentionally does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence effects, session or execution‑time errors, hardware resource limits, or subtle environment side effects; passing the verifier is therefore necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient to guarantee production safety. Expanding verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence models) is required before operational automation.

Operational implications and cost tradeoffs: A compact deterministic verifier plus a bounded repair loop intercepted verifier‑detectable hazards at low LLM overhead in this synthetic workload. Observed repair rate was 4/500 (0.8%), implying modest additional model calls under the bounded policy: observed hosted model call events = 504 with stage counts of 500 shared initial and 4 repair calls. In operations this pattern suggests that a low‑latency verifier integrated as a gate can materially reduce verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at modest model‑call cost when baseline failure rates are low. Real deployments must measure verifier runtime on full inventories, evaluate how repair frequency scales under adversarial or more diverse intent distributions, and balance the latency/cost of higher‑fidelity verifiers against residual operational risk.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, fixed seeds, and complete accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; no failed episodes). Construct validity is limited by the verifier's abstraction level and by the synthetic device templates: the verifier enforces encoded workflow and group constraints that match the synthetic intent grammar, but those rules are an imperfect model of vendor behavior and control‑plane dynamics. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication, vendor‑specific parsing, and live telemetry tests are required to generalize. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan assumed a larger baseline failure rate and targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08; the observed near‑ceiling baseline (496/500 = 0.992) yielded only four discordant pairs and reduced realized power relative to the preregistered assumption. These limitations explain why a modest numerical paired difference appears in the exploratory bootstrap interval but not in the preregistered exact McNemar decision.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (which was not executed in this run). Full machine‑readable execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
